clue.text: Companions, of royalty on talks agenda ?

definitions.text: Companions, of royalty on talks agenda ?

parts.words: Companions, of royalty on talks agenda ?
parts.note: in Lewis Carroll's Walrus and the Carpenter the Walrus proposes to talk of shoes and ships and sealing-wax, of these vegetables and kings, so they keep royal company on the agenda

explanation.surface: A question about who accompanies the monarchy on a list of items for negotiation.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'talks agenda' is the Walrus's list in Through the Looking-Glass: 'of cabbages and kings', where the vegetables sit right beside royalty.
explanation.definitionFit: In Carroll's famous line the vegetables are paired with kings, making them literary companions of royalty.

clue.text: Brecon, Dorchester — both accommodate this bird

indicators.note: the two town names between them house the bird's letters, spanning the join

explanation.surface: Two British towns both play host to a particular bird.
explanation.walkthrough: Brecon is a Welsh town, Dorchester an English county town; the bird straddles the end of one and the start of the other.
explanation.definitionFit: A large South American vulture with a huge wingspan.

clue.text: Overdone quality ?

parts.note: overdone hints at excess, and the quality meant is a lewdness, as if being done over by a madam of a brothel

explanation.surface: A remark on something exaggerated.
explanation.walkthrough: A whimsical definition: a bawd keeps a brothel, so the quality of being 'over-done' (too much) is read as a racy, indecent one.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means obscenity or lewd humour, a quality thought excessive in polite company.

clue.text: Deadly sin holds artist back in a firm grip

indicators.note: something that holds another thing keeps it inside, so the reversed painter goes within

parts.note: a vice is a clamp that gives a firm grip

indicators.note: back means the painter abbreviation is read from its end

parts.note: RA, Royal Academician, is an artist

explanation.surface: Greed keeps a painter held tightly in a clamp.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns RA to AR, and 'holds' puts AR inside A VICE.
explanation.definitionFit: Greed for wealth is one of the seven cardinal sins.

clue.text: No odds, still, on Sultan's Head

parts.note: even can mean still, as in even more

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, here of the ruler's name

explanation.surface: A betting tip says no odds are offered on the sultan's chief.
explanation.definitionFit: In betting, even money means a stake wins only its own amount, with no advantage in the odds.

clue.text: Cut in vessel replacements

indicators.note: the word in tells us the trimming verb goes inside the ship abbreviation

parts.note: SS, steamship, stands for a vessel
to pare is to cut or trim

explanation.surface: A slash found in a ship's spare parts.
explanation.definitionFit: Spares are extra parts kept to stand in for broken ones, i.e. substitutes.

clue.text: Forecast electoral system order

parts.note: PR is proportional representation, a voting system
an edict is an official order

explanation.surface: A voting scheme ordered to be predicted.
explanation.definitionFit: To foretell or prophesy what will happen.

clue.text: Had no mount for this show

parts.note: had a mount, i.e. sat on horseback, gives the past tense of the riding verb
O, the zero shape, means no or nothing

explanation.surface: A rider without a horse for the event.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'Had ... mount' as RODE, with 'no' for O placed after it; the surface suggests the opposite, a rider left horseless.
explanation.definitionFit: A rodeo is a public exhibition of cowboy skills, a spectacle or performance.

clue.text: In song, one unknown in paradise

definitions.text: In song, one unknown in paradise

parts.words: In song, one unknown in paradise
parts.note: the musical Kismet has the hit '... in Paradise', whose title figure is someone unfamiliar

explanation.surface: A lyric about an unknown person in heaven.
explanation.walkthrough: Stranger in Paradise is a popular song from the 1953 musical Kismet.
explanation.definitionFit: An unfamiliar person, someone not known to you, as in the song title.

clue.text: Those whom Jones, P., keeps changing

definitions.text: Those whom Jones, P., keeps changing

parts.words: Those whom Jones, P., keeps changing
parts.note: a person who swaps dance or business companions keeps changing these associates

explanation.surface: A gossip note about the people a certain Jones keeps swapping.
explanation.walkthrough: A light cryptic definition: people often 'change partners' at a dance; the made-up P. Jones is just a typical person.
explanation.definitionFit: Associates or companions in dance, marriage or business.

clue.text: Cadge a tenner ?- law broken by criminals

indicators.note: a law that is broken is violated, and here the letters before it are smashed and reassembled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone begging ten pounds, with the law flouted by crooks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broken' rearranges CADGE A TENNER LAW. The Newgate Calendar was a popular 18th–19th-century collection of the lives of notorious criminals held in London's Newgate prison, so the definition stands for the book by its subject.
explanation.definitionFit: The title names a famous anthology recording the crimes and fates of felons, so it is loosely defined by its subjects, the lawbreakers.

clue.text: Sources which make one grin so

indicators.note: to make the following letters into something new signals a rearrangement of them

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I
taken as written

explanation.surface: Things that can make a person smile like that.
explanation.definitionFit: Sources are where things begin, their beginnings or roots.

clue.text: Test cereal ?. My hat!

parts.note: to test is to try, and cereal can be corn; said together these make a three-cornered piece of headgear, and My hat! names the category

explanation.surface: Someone sampling a breakfast cereal exclaims in surprise.
explanation.walkthrough: A pun with no sound signal: TRY (test) + CORN (cereal) is pronounced like the hat, and 'My hat!' doubles as an old exclamation of surprise.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a hat with its brim turned up on three sides, worn in the eighteenth century.

clue.text: Representative of French Ambassador

parts.note: de is French for of
a legate is an envoy, especially a papal ambassador

explanation.surface: A diplomat acting for the French envoy.
explanation.definitionFit: A delegate is a person sent to act or vote on behalf of others.

clue.text: He travelled amongst wild Sudan men

indicators.note: something wild is untamed and disordered, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An explorer moving among untamed Sudanese tribesmen.
explanation.walkthrough: Roald Amundsen, the Norwegian explorer, was first to the South Pole.
explanation.definitionFit: The Norwegian polar explorer was famous for his journeys, first to reach the South Pole in 1911.

clue.text: Article about that place

parts.note: the definite article
re means about or concerning

explanation.surface: A newspaper piece concerning some location.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is an adverb meaning in or at a spot other than here.

clue.text: An explosive device in East Street Junction cafe

indicators.note: the word in places the weapon phrase inside the run of street abbreviations

parts.note: E is east
ST is street
T for a T-junction
a mine is an explosive device

explanation.surface: A bomb planted in a café at an East Street crossroads.
explanation.definitionFit: An estaminet is a small French café or bar selling alcohol.

clue.text: Borders of Virginia needing weapons

parts.note: VA is the US state abbreviation for Virginia
lances are spear-like weapons

explanation.surface: The frontiers of a US state demanding arms.
explanation.definitionFit: Valances are short drapes or frills hung along the edge of a bed or window, decorative edgings.

clue.text: Like Pepys country

parts.note: as means like
Samuel Pepys, the diarist, shortened to Sam

explanation.surface: Something resembling the diarist's homeland.
explanation.definitionFit: Assam is a region of north-east India famous for tea, a tract of land or territory.

clue.text: Add up to one state- Oklahoma, perhaps

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the totalling word is read from the bottom

parts.note: to add is to sum
one is the Roman numeral I
Cal is short for California

explanation.surface: Totalling the figures for one American state, Oklahoma.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns SUM into MUS. Oklahoma! is a Rodgers and Hammerstein stage show, not here the state.
explanation.definitionFit: Oklahoma! is a classic example of a stage show with songs.

clue.text: They come from humble but well-informed beginnings

parts.note: to be up on something is to be well-informed about it
starts are beginnings

explanation.surface: People of modest origins who are nonetheless knowledgeable.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition runs into 'beginnings', which seems to finish it; 'but' joins it to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: An upstart is someone newly risen from low status who behaves arrogantly, so such people come from lowly origins.

clue.text: Scared Capone with guns

parts.note: Al Capone, the Chicago gangster
armed means carrying weapons

explanation.surface: Frightened by the gangster carrying firearms.
explanation.definitionFit: Frightened, filled with fear or anxiety.

clue.text: Man in plot sounded asinine

indicators.note: in means the name goes inside the garden plot

parts.note: a bed is a plot of garden
Ray is a man's name

explanation.surface: A man in a scheme made a foolish noise.
explanation.definitionFit: Asinine means donkey-like; making a donkey's cry is to hee-haw.

clue.text: Charged a small amount to American journalist

parts.note: cc, a cubic centimetre, is a small measure
ed, short for editor, is a crossword journalist

explanation.surface: Billing an American reporter a modest sum.
explanation.definitionFit: To be charged with a crime is to be formally indicted of it.

clue.text: One knowing all prices but no values (Wilde)

definitions.text: One knowing all prices but no values (Wilde)

parts.words: One knowing all prices but no values (Wilde)
parts.note: Oscar Wilde defined such a person as 'a man who knows the price of everything and the value of nothing'

explanation.surface: A quotation from Wilde about someone who knows costs but not worth.
explanation.walkthrough: The line is from Lady Windermere's Fan.
explanation.definitionFit: A sceptic who doubts the sincerity of others' motives, as Wilde described.

clue.text: One of two Macheath could be happy with

definitions.text: One of two Macheath could be happy with

parts.words: One of two Macheath could be happy with
parts.note: in Gay's Beggar's Opera the highwayman Macheath sings 'How happy could I be with either, were t'other dear' one away, about his two sweethearts

explanation.surface: A remark about which of two women the highwayman might settle with.
explanation.walkthrough: Macheath, the hero of John Gay's The Beggar's Opera, sings of his two loves Polly and Lucy, ending each with 'were t'other dear charmer away'.
explanation.definitionFit: The song calls each of his sweethearts a delightful enchantress, the word Gay used for a beloved woman.

clue.text: Two officers take a drink

parts.note: CO is a commanding officer
a second commanding officer

explanation.surface: A pair of officers having a drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A hot beverage made from cacao powder.

clue.text: A sorry (Hamlet might say cowardly ?) payment

definitions.text: A sorry (Hamlet might say cowardly ?) payment

parts.words: A sorry (Hamlet might say cowardly ?) payment
parts.note: Hamlet says that thinking about right and wrong 'does make cowards of us all', so a guilt-driven payment could be called cowardly cash by him

explanation.surface: A regretful payment that Shakespeare's prince might call craven.
explanation.walkthrough: Hamlet's soliloquy: 'Thus conscience does make cowards of us all'. Money paid to ease a guilty conscience is therefore, in his terms, cowardly.
explanation.definitionFit: It is money paid anonymously out of guilt, such as for unpaid taxes, by someone feeling remorse.

clue.text: Harvester causes " Just so " animal to return

parts.note: sic, Latin for thus, marks a quotation as just so

indicators.note: to return is to come back, so the animal's name is read from its end

parts.note: an elk is a large deer

explanation.surface: A farm worker or machine making a beast go back, apparently thus.
explanation.definitionFit: A curved blade used for cutting crops, a reaping tool.

clue.text: Fellow has old-fashioned description of trust territories

parts.note: a fellow is a man
dated means out of fashion

explanation.surface: A man with a dated way of describing administered lands.
explanation.definitionFit: After WWI the League of Nations gave colonies to powers under a mandate, so such trust territories were described by this adjective.
